article.title: Anti-austerity protests continue with force in France
article.author: Ana Vračar
article.content: Half a million people took part in demonstrations across France on Tuesday, November 17, in response to a strike call by public sector workers. Tuesday’s strike and protests marked the continuation of a mobilization wave that has shaken the country for approximately two months. “Today was the eleventh round of demonstrations since September 29,” wrote the General Confederation of Labor (CGT). “All in all, in two months, over 5 million demonstrators joined the mobilization for our public services and against the cost of living crisis.” Watch: France’s protest movement is fighting more than Macron “Workers continue to demonstrate their rejection of austerity policies, the deterioration of public services and the erosion of purchasing power,” echoed the trade union organization Solidaires . “Sébastien Lecornu’s announcements at Matignon reinforced the anger and determination to achieve our demands. Meanwhile, the salaries of big bosses are soaring!” Workers say crumbs proposed by government are an affront While the scale of mobilizations over the past weeks appears to have dented the government’s stance, trade unions emphasize that the measures ministers are bringing to the table are far from enough. “The crumbs proposed by David Amiel and Sébastien Lecornu are an affront,” two Solidaires activists said during Tuesday’s protests. “Five-euro pay raises – barely enough to buy a couple more baguettes each month. Public sector workers numbering in the hundreds of thousands stuck below the minimum wage. And an index point for calculating pay that remains frozen.” “Half a million people who took to the streets today prove it – our anger continues to grow, and real solutions need to come to the table.” Students continue to march with trade unions High school and university students once again joined the unions’ mobilization call, reiterating the links between workers’ demands for salary increases and their own demands for more investment in public education and infrastructure, the abolition of the recruitment platform Parcoursup, and more university placements. Read more: Students in France are fighting for stronger public education Echoing workers refusing the crumbs offered by the Lecornu administration while management and shareholder income continues to rise, students insisted they would keep fighting until their full list of demands was met. “We’re not asking for the moon, just the bare minimum for education,” wrote the high school student union Union Syndicale Lycéenne (USL). “Our determination is not waning, quite the contrary,” they said . “It’s time to get a political response adequate to our demands.” Mobilizations to continue throughout November Ahead of the most recent day of action, high school and university students once again faced attempts to prevent their mobilization. In Paris, authorities announced that “unannounced actions” – meaning student blockades – would be banned. Police forces could be seen in Nelson Mandela High School in Nantes on November 16 during education minister’s Édouard Geffray visit. Photo: Union Étudiante/Instagram The measure, however, was quickly struck down in administrative court – and students are already preparing for new mobilizations over the weekend. “Many new steps have already been announced,” the CGT wrote. “Thursday, November 19, a national demonstration of retirees; Friday, November 20, with the youth’s call for a European day of action; Saturday, November 21, with a day of mobilization against the cost of living crisis; and Saturday, November 28, with the international day of action for the elimination of gender-based violence.”
